q: Q1. Our depolarizing-only replication got clean O(eps), O(eps^2), O(eps^3) scaling for raw, ZNE1, and ZNE2 (slopes 1.00 / 2.00 / 2.99 on eps in [1e-4, 1e-3]). The paper's Fig. 1(b) amplitude-damping / dephasing curves visibly flatten out at higher noise than the depolarizing curves. Does the O(lambda^{n+1}) scaling law hold with the same prefactor for non-unital channels, or does the amplitude-damping steady-state bias push a channel-specific correction into the leading remainder R_{n+1}?
basis: Only depolarizing noise was tested. The Richardson theorem in the paper is stated for any weak, time-scale-invariant L(rho), but non-unital channels behave differently under global rescaling and this is not exercised in our sweep.
next_steps: Extend zne_replication.py to swap the depolarizing_error() for amplitude_damping_error(c*T1_ratio) and phase_damping_error(c*T2_ratio); repeat the slope fit; compare prefactors and the eps* at which the scaling breaks down.

q: Q2. We scaled noise by simply rebuilding a Qiskit NoiseModel at rate c*epsilon. On real hardware the paper's rescaling protocol (Eq. 5) requires physically slowing the pulses by c and re-calibrating gates. Does 'gate-duration folding' (repeat each gate c times) reproduce ZNE with the same order-of-cancellation as our exact digital rescaling, or does per-gate overhead / calibration drift eat one order?
basis: Our slopes matched theory to 3 decimal places because our noise rescaling is EXACT — a luxury unavailable on hardware. Popular open-source implementations (Mitiq, IBM Qiskit-Runtime) instead use pulse-stretching or unitary-folding as proxies, whose fidelity to Eq. 5 is not directly benchmarked in this paper.
next_steps: Repeat the sweep using Mitiq's unitary-folding scaler against the same depolarizing noise model; compare slopes to our clean 1/2/3 baseline; the gap quantifies the folding-vs-true-rescaling overhead.

q: Q3. At eps = 1e-2 our ZNE2 still won 8/8 vs ZNE1 but the improvement ratio (raw/ZNE2 = 60x) is dramatically smaller than at eps = 1e-3 (raw/ZNE2 = 5000x). Where exactly is the crossover between the perturbative regime (Richardson wins big) and the regime where the higher-order terms in the Born-series remainder start to dominate? Can we predict the optimal n for a given (epsilon, depth) budget from first principles?
basis: The paper's bound |E* - E_hat^n_K| <= (l_{n+1} (lambda T)^{n+1}) / (n+1)! * (product of gamma_j 's) shows that increasing n eventually hurts because of the growing coefficient sum. Our data shows the leading behavior but does not map the crossover.
next_steps: Sweep n from 1 to 5 (c = 1..n+1) at each of 5 epsilon values, plot mean-err vs n; the U-shape in n identifies n_opt(eps); compare to the paper's analytic bound.

q: Q4. Our observable was a fixed <Z_0 Z_1>. The paper's Fig. 1 aggregates over 'randomly chosen multi-qubit Pauli operators P_alpha' at each circuit realization. Does the ZNE improvement factor depend on the weight/support of the observable? Concretely, do global Paulis (weight-N) mitigate worse than local ones because the noise couples more paths?
basis: We fixed a weight-2 observable to keep the run cheap. The paper reports averages over random Pauli measurements but does not break down the improvement by observable weight.
next_steps: Modify z0z1_expectation() to loop over all 4^N - 1 Paulis, tabulate improvement vs Pauli weight, look for a scaling law of the form improvement ~ c^(-w * n) for weight w.

q: Q5. The Richardson coefficients (2,-1) and (3,-3,1) have L1-norm 3 and 7 respectively — the paper notes this becomes a variance-amplification cost when moving from exact expectation values to shot-based estimates. Our density-matrix sim has zero shot noise so this cost is invisible. What sample-count budget T_shots would make ZNE2 stop beating ZNE1 at each of our five noise rates?
basis: Real hardware uses shots; the paper's Eq. (3) says the variance of the ZNE estimator scales like (sum |gamma_j|)^2 / T_shots, but no numerical variance curve is shown. Our replication cannot see this because it is shot-free.
next_steps: Rerun the sweep with AerSimulator method='statevector' + finite shots (shots in {100, 1e3, 1e4, 1e5}); plot bias-variance-tradeoff curves; identify the shots* below which the higher-variance ZNE2 loses to the lower-bias ZNE1 in mean-squared error.
